posts.title: Occultism: a voice agent that talks for ₹2 a minute
posts.author: Shaurya Garg
posts.intro: A real-time voice agent for astrology consultations, in Hindi and English — and a bakeoff of six speech models to find out what a minute of talking actually costs.
posts.quote: Talk-minutes are the whole bill. Once I logged cost per turn, the architecture decisions made themselves.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.body:
Occultism is a voice-agent platform: callers speak naturally over WebRTC, in Hindi, English or Hinglish, and a live speech model answers. Harder questions are routed to a reasoning LLM fallback, masked behind filler speech so the call never goes silent.

Agents are config-driven. An Agent Builder lets you pick the model, prompt and tools — HTTP tools, LLM tools and built-ins like deep_analysis and end_call — without touching code.

sections.heading: Six models, 124 calls
sections.body:
I ran a head-to-head bakeoff across OpenAI Realtime, Gemini Live and a cascaded Sarvam STT → LLM → TTS pipeline, logging every turn's latency, tokens and cost.

The Sarvam cascade won on price: about ₹2/min ($0.023/min), 48% cheaper than Gemini Live. Median voice round-trip across calls was 1.38 s, under the 1.5 s target. Text-to-speech turned out to be ~80% of the Sarvam bill, which tells you where to optimise next.

sections.heading: Under the hood
sections.body:
An async Python backend built on LiveKit Agents, with per-turn SQLite logging, a usage and cost-per-call dashboard, call recordings, silence nudges and max-length hang-ups. SSRF-guarded HTTP tools, a pytest suite, and a Docker Compose stack self-hosted on my own server behind Cloudflare Tunnels.

Stack: Python, LiveKit, OpenAI Realtime, Gemini Live, Sarvam, Next.js, Docker.

posts.title: Irregs: beating Ollama with a from-scratch C++ LLM engine
posts.author: Shaurya Garg
posts.intro: No PyTorch, no llama.cpp, no ML libraries — just C++ and one model, TinyLlama-1.1B. The goal: catch Ollama on a CPU.
posts.quote: Decode is a memory-bandwidth problem. Every byte of weight you don't stream is speed you get for free.

sections.heading: Starting slow
sections.body:
Irregs (built with @FloatingComet62) implements the whole stack by hand: mmap weight loading, the tokenizer, the Llama transformer forward pass and the KV cache, verified token-for-token against a reference implementation.

The fp32 baseline streamed 4.4 GB of weights per token and decoded at 3.3 tokens/s. Ollama did 22.8.

sections.heading: Closing the gap
sections.body:
Profiling showed matmul was ~95% of runtime, so that's where the work went: INT4 quantization, SIMD kernels, fusion and threading.

Decode went from 3.3 to 60.9 tokens/s — 18.5× faster — and the model shrank 6.7× (4.1 GB → 615 MB) for only +0.5% perplexity. At 4 threads it beats Ollama (llama.cpp) by 7%, matches it at 8, and uses 12% less peak RAM. Prefill is still Ollama's win — that's next.

sections.heading: A fair fight
sections.body:
A benchmark harness gives both engines the same prompts, chat template, greedy decoding and thread count, with a warm-up and fresh prompts each run so Ollama's prompt cache can't skip prefill. It tracks decode and prefill speed, TTFT, perplexity, energy per token and memory-bandwidth utilisation, saved per commit.

Stack: C++17, OpenMP, SIMD, INT4 quantization.

posts.title: WarRoom: a live case competition run by LLMs
posts.author: Shaurya Garg
posts.intro: A real-time case competition platform for 32–40 teams, where strategies are graded by an LLM and every team can trade stock in everyone else's company.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body:
Teams submit strategy decisions, an LLM evaluates them, and a human-in-the-loop step validates the scores before they hit the board. Meanwhile a live market lets teams trade stock in each other's companies, so every evaluation moves prices in real time.

Code: github.com/Shauryaroks/WarRoom

posts.title: free-code: routing work to the cheapest coding agent
posts.author: Shaurya Garg
posts.intro: Why pay for the biggest coding agent on every step when a cheaper one might pass the tests?

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body:
free-code runs coding-agent CLIs in parallel across git worktrees. Each step is routed to the cheapest agent that passes its test gate, so expensive models only get the work cheaper ones fail.

Code: github.com/Shauryaroks/free-code

posts.title: Event Complex: an LLM-run market for 50 companies
posts.author: Shaurya Garg
posts.intro: What happens when 50 companies make strategic decisions in real time and an LLM runs the market? I built the engine that found out.
posts.quote: The hardest part wasn't the AI — it was keeping 100+ people's decisions consistent while the LLMs churned in the background.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.body:
Event Complex is an LLM-powered consulting and market simulation platform. Teams representing 50 simulated companies make strategic business decisions that move company valuation, stock prices, and assets — all in real time.

Instead of a static case study, every choice a team makes feeds back into a living market that the other teams then have to react to.

sections.heading: The hard part: scale
sections.body:
The backend had to support 100+ concurrent users while orchestrating load-balanced LLM API calls and synchronizing real-time state across every team.

I built it on async FastAPI endpoints and WebSockets, with request orchestration so no single LLM call blocked the room, and a PostgreSQL-backed state layer that stayed consistent even as dozens of decisions landed at once.

sections.heading: What I built
sections.body:
A decision-evaluation pipeline runs each team's strategy through LLM-driven workflows to dynamically simulate the market and business outcomes.

Stack: Python, FastAPI, PostgreSQL, LLM APIs, WebSockets.

posts.title: Perplexed: four C-suite chatbots for 200+ people
posts.author: Shaurya Garg
posts.intro: An AI consulting and audit simulation that put 200+ participants in a room with a company's entire executive team — except the executives were LLMs.

sections.heading: The setup
sections.body:
Built for Saturnalia, Perplexed hosted 200+ participants diagnosing real problem statements and building case solutions through realistic executive interactions.

Each participant could interrogate the leadership, and the leadership answered like the people who actually run the company.

sections.heading: Grounding the personas
sections.body:
I engineered an LLM backend of 4 distinct chatbots, each simulating a different C-suite persona. To keep them from hallucinating, every persona runs on a RAG pipeline: company documents are chunked, embedded and indexed in FAISS and Pinecone, then retrieved through LangChain at answer time.

So the CFO answered from the financials, the CTO from the tech docs — retrieval-augmented, not made up.

sections.heading: The frontend
sections.body:
I built the full Next.js / TanStack frontend and wired Google Gemini API calls for the simulated executive responses.

Stack: Next.js, TanStack, LangChain, FAISS, Pinecone, Google Gemini.

posts.title: CitySaver: teaching buildings to share power
posts.author: Shaurya Garg
posts.intro: A real-time microgrid simulation where multiple buildings learn to coordinate energy decisions — and cut carbon by doing it.

sections.heading: The problem
sections.body:
Buildings consume power, generate solar, and emit carbon independently. Left alone, they don't coordinate — and the grid pays for it.

I wanted to model what happens when they cooperate.

sections.heading: Multi-agent reinforcement learning
sections.body:
Using the CityLearn environment, I built a platform that models energy consumption, solar generation, and carbon emissions across multiple buildings.

Then I integrated a Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning system (GridHarmony) so buildings coordinate energy decisions for grid-level optimization — reaching a 2.51% improvement in carbon emissions.

sections.heading: Under the hood
sections.body:
A simulation engine computes building-level consumption, renewable utilization, and carbon emissions from real dataset timesteps.

Stack: Python, FastAPI, CityLearn, MARL, WebSockets.

posts.title: KAIRA: building a robot that knows who it's talking to
posts.author: Shaurya Garg
posts.intro: Say "Hey KAIRA" and a robot wakes up, recognises your face, and answers from what it actually knows. Here's how it comes together.

sections.heading: Wake, see, respond
sections.body:
KAIRA is a Satbot project: a robot with a RAG architecture that recognises people and communicates, activated by the wake phrase "Hey KAIRA".

Computer vision handles the recognition; retrieval-augmented generation handles the answers, so it responds from a real knowledge base instead of guessing.

sections.heading: Reliable communication
sections.body:
The pieces talk over a Subscriber-Publisher architecture with socket-based communication for reliable, real-time interaction — so vision, speech, and the language model stay in sync without stepping on each other.

I also contributed to the design and development of the robot's user interface.

Stack: RAG, Pub-Sub architecture, sockets, computer vision.
